R08-D-01: Every generation of reformers discovers that words wear out. A term introduced to replace a cruder one, chosen precisely because it carried none of the old contempt, acquires that contempt within a few decades, and a new term is proposed to replace it in turn. Students of language sometimes call this cycle a treadmill, and the image is apt: a great deal of effort is expended, and the speaker seems to remain in the same place. Words for bodily functions, for old age, for poverty and for conditions of the mind have all passed through several such rotations, each new coinage arriving clean and departing stained. The usual explanation is that the stain was never in the word. Attitudes towards the thing named are what give a word its colouring, and so long as those attitudes persist, any word that reliably points at the thing will soon absorb them. On this view the replacement of terms is a kind of displacement activity, a way of feeling that something has been done while the underlying attitude goes untouched. Critics who hold this view tend to conclude that the whole enterprise of renaming is futile, and some go further and call it dishonest, since the fresh term flatters the speaker as much as it spares the listener. The first half of this argument seems to me largely right, and the second half too hasty. It is true that a new word cannot by itself change what people feel about the thing it names. But the treadmill is not simply a record of failure. A replacement term, for the years before it darkens, often gives people a way of speaking about a subject without signalling contempt, and in that interval conversations become possible that were not possible before. A parent can ask a teacher about a child's difficulty in terms that do not insult the child; an official form can ask about a condition without reading like an accusation. These are small goods, but they are not nothing, and they are purchased cheaply. What the treadmill does show is that renaming cannot carry the whole burden of reform. A society that changes its vocabulary for poverty while leaving the poor exactly as they were will find that its new word sours as fast as the old one, and perhaps faster, since the gap between the gentle name and the harsh reality invites irony. The cycle slows, where it slows at all, when the thing named stops being a mark of shame. The word then has nothing to absorb. Renaming is best understood not as a substitute for that change but as a temporary courtesy that can accompany it.
R08-D-02: Public life has an elaborate culture of speaking and almost none of listening. Schools hold debating contests, organisations train their staff in presentation, and the history of rhetoric is largely a history of techniques for the person holding the floor. Listening, by contrast, is treated as what happens automatically when someone else is talking, a passive condition rather than an activity. Nobody is coached in it, and nobody wins a prize for it. This neglect would matter less if listening were in fact passive. It is not. To follow an argument one disagrees with, a person has to hold its parts in mind long enough to see how they connect, resist the urge to compose a reply while the speaker is still in the middle of a sentence, and notice the difference between what was said and what one expected to hear. Each of these is effortful, and each can be done well or badly. Anyone who has watched a meeting in which three people answer a point that nobody made has seen what happens when it is done badly. One objection is that a culture of listening would favour the patient over the right. If every view must be heard out in full, the argument runs, then bad ideas gain a hearing they have not earned, and those who are merely persistent will exhaust everyone else. There is something to this. Listening is not the same as agreeing, and a meeting that cannot end because everyone must be fully heard is not a model of deliberation. But the objection mistakes the purpose. Careful listening is valuable less because it is fair to the speaker than because it is useful to the listener: a person who has understood an opposing view can answer the strongest form of it, and can sometimes discover that the disagreement was smaller than it looked. Nor is it obvious that listening must be slow. Much of the time lost in public argument is lost to misunderstanding, to replies aimed at positions no one holds and to corrections of those replies. A discussion in which each participant first restated the other's point before answering it might take longer at each step and less time overall. If that is so, the case for teaching listening is not a plea for patience but a practical one, and it is odd that institutions so devoted to efficient communication have left half of communication untaught.
R08-D-03: It has become a commonplace that the internet would be a more civil place if people had to speak under their own names. The reasoning is simple: a person who cannot be identified bears no cost for cruelty, and a person who bears no cost will be cruel more often. Proposals to require verified identities on public platforms rest on this reasoning, and it has an obvious appeal to anyone who has read the comments beneath a news article. The reasoning is not wrong so much as incomplete. Anonymity does loosen some restraints; people say things to a faceless audience that they would not say across a table. But the restraint that matters most in face-to-face life is not the fear of being named. It is the expectation of meeting the same people again. A villager who insults a neighbour must live beside her the next day; a commuter who insults a stranger on a train usually need not, and commuters are not famous for their courtesy. What disinhibits is less the absence of a name than the absence of a future in which one's words will have to be lived with. Seen this way, the relevant distinction online is not between named and anonymous accounts but between identities that are durable and identities that are disposable. A pseudonym used for years in a small forum accumulates a reputation as surely as a name does, and its owner has much to lose by squandering it. Many such forums are known for patient and generous discussion, though few of their members could be identified by an outsider. Conversely, people posting under their real names on large platforms frequently behave badly, perhaps because the audience is so vast and transient that no particular reader's opinion of them seems to count. None of this shows that identity requirements would do nothing. They might deter some of the worst abuse, and they would make legal remedies easier to pursue. But they carry costs that fall unevenly. The people with most to fear from being named are not usually the trolls; they are the employee describing misconduct at work, the young person asking about a matter their family would punish, the dissenter in a place where dissent is dangerous. A policy that removes their cover in order to inconvenience the cruel has chosen a blunt instrument where a finer one was available: designing spaces in which identities, named or not, persist long enough to matter.
R08-D-04: Imagine a photograph of a cat staring with great solemnity at an empty food bowl. In its first appearance the caption beneath it complains, in the cat's voice, about a late breakfast. Within days the same photograph carries hundreds of other captions: a student staring at an exam paper, an investor staring at a falling share price, a voter staring at a ballot. The cat, and the bowl, have stopped meaning anything about cats. They have become a frame into which almost any experience of disappointed expectation can be placed. This is the ordinary life of an internet meme, and it is worth noticing what has actually spread. It is not a message, since the messages are all different and many contradict one another. What has spread is a template: a recognisable structure with a slot in it, together with a tacit rule about what kind of thing goes in the slot. Those who share the meme are not endorsing a claim; they are demonstrating that they know the form and can fill it aptly. The pleasure is the pleasure of a good fit, much like the pleasure an audience once took in a skilled performer's handling of a familiar tale, where the interest lay less in what happened than in how well the expected moves were made. This has consequences for how memes are read by those who study public opinion. It is tempting to treat the reach of a political meme as a measure of agreement with it, as if each share were a small vote. But a template can carry a sentiment its sharers do not hold, simply because the sentiment fits the slot neatly, and a meme that mocks one side may be passed along by the other side in an inverted version that keeps the frame and reverses the point. Counting shares, in such cases, measures the vitality of the form far more reliably than the distribution of belief. It would be too quick to conclude that memes persuade nobody. Repetition has effects, and a frame that is used often enough can make one way of seeing a situation feel natural before anyone has argued for it. If the cat's bowl is used a thousand times to describe a particular government's policies, the idea that those policies are a disappointment may come to seem like common knowledge. But the persuasive power, where it exists, lies in the frame's quiet familiarity rather than in any argument, and it is precisely because memes do not look like arguments that their influence is so hard to measure and so easy to misread.
R08-D-05: Two attitudes to the character of the speaker run through the study of persuasion, and they are hard to reconcile. The first, familiar from introductory logic, holds that an argument stands or falls on its own terms. Who makes it is irrelevant; to reject a claim because of the person advancing it is to commit a fallacy, and to accept a claim because of the person is the same error in a friendlier mood. The second attitude is older. Aristotle counted the character of the speaker among the means of persuasion, alongside appeals to the emotions of the audience and to the argument itself, and he did not present it as a regrettable weakness of listeners. A speaker who seems sensible, honest and well disposed towards the audience is, on this view, more worthy of belief, and an audience is right to take that into account. The logician's attitude is correct for a particular situation: one in which the listener can examine the argument fully. A proof in geometry is no better for coming from a famous mathematician. But most of the claims on which people must act are not like proofs. A patient cannot check a diagnosis, a juror cannot repeat the forensic analysis, and a citizen cannot audit the statistics behind a policy. In such cases the listener is not choosing between evaluating the argument and evaluating the speaker; the argument is largely out of reach, and the speaker's record, competence and incentives are the best evidence available. To attend to them is not a lapse in reasoning but reasoning under a division of intellectual labour that no one can escape. If this rehabilitates the appeal to character, it also shows where that appeal goes wrong. Credibility is earned in a domain. The physician's record is evidence about diagnoses, not about tax policy, and the honesty of a popular broadcaster is evidence that he reports what he believes, not that what he believes is true. Much modern persuasion works by carrying trust from the place where it was earned to a place where it has no bearing: the athlete who recommends an investment, the scientist who pronounces on matters far from her field. The listener who accepts such claims is not wrong to rely on character in general; she is wrong about which character she is relying on. The two attitudes, then, are less opposed than they first appear. The logician is right that character cannot make a bad argument good, and the rhetorician is right that, where arguments cannot be inspected, character is often all a listener has to go on. What a careful audience needs is neither a rule against attending to the speaker nor a habit of trusting the likeable, but the narrower discipline of asking what, exactly, the speaker's credibility is credibility about.
R08-D-06: Spoken irony rarely needs announcing. A slight drag on a word, a flattened pitch, a pause before the punchline: listeners pick up such cues without noticing that they have done so, and the speaker relies on them without noticing either. Writing, however expressive in other respects, strips most of them away. For centuries this mattered less than it might have, because the written forms people used for personal exchange, letters above all, were slow, composed and long enough to establish their own tone over several paragraphs. A letter writer who wished to be ironic had room to prepare the reader for it. The short typed message removes that room while keeping the pace of speech. Exchanges happen in seconds, between people who often know each other well enough to joke, in fragments too brief to carry their own context. The result is a familiar variety of communicative accident. A remark meant as affectionate teasing arrives as a rebuke; a dry agreement reads as sincere enthusiasm, or the reverse. The writer, who heard the intended tone in his own head as he typed, is often the last to see that it was not on the screen. Writers have not, however, accepted this deprivation quietly. Over the past few decades they have built, without any committee to guide them, a supplementary system of signals: the small faces and symbols that can be appended to a sentence, the strategic use of capitals and repeated letters, even the presence or absence of a full stop, which among some groups of writers has come to make a short reply sound curt. It is common to lament these devices as a decline in the standards of written language. That complaint misses what they are for. They are not a lazy substitute for vocabulary but a written prosody, an attempt to restore precisely the cues that typing removed. Yet the new system has a weakness that spoken prosody largely lacks. The meaning of a rising tone is shared across most speakers of a language; the meaning of a particular symbol or a missing full stop is settled within smaller circles and changes quickly. A face that one group uses to soften a criticism may strike another as mocking, and a message read across a gap of age or community can misfire precisely because the writer took care to mark its tone. The invention of written prosody, in other words, has not abolished misreading so much as relocated it, from the gap between voice and text to the gap between the conventions of different readers.
R08-D-07: Critics of political language have long treated the slogan as its lowest form. A slogan, they point out, asserts nothing that could be checked. Words such as renewal, fairness, security or change are compatible with almost any programme, and a campaign that rallies behind one of them has, in effect, declined to say what it will do. On this account the vagueness of the slogan is a species of evasion, and the remedy is to demand specifics: costed proposals, timetables, named measures that a voter can hold against the candidate once the votes have been counted. There is a good deal of sense in this, but it rests on a picture of the voter as an individual buyer comparing the contents of rival packages. Politics in most large societies does not work like that. A party seeking a majority must assemble people whose interests and hopes overlap only partly: the worker and the small employer, the city and the countryside, the young and the retired. A precise programme would divide them at once, since each specific measure pleases some members of the coalition at the expense of others. A slogan holds them together by offering a phrase into which each can read a version of what he or she wants. Its emptiness is not a failure of communication; it is what allows a heterogeneous coalition to communicate with itself at all. To see the slogan in this way is not to absolve it, for the difficulty has merely been postponed. A coalition assembled on an open phrase must, once it wins, translate the phrase into decisions, and each decision closes off some of the readings that brought supporters in. Those whose reading is closed off do not usually feel that a compromise has been struck; they feel that a promise has been broken, and in a sense they are right, since the slogan let each of them believe that it had been made to them. The disillusionment that so regularly follows electoral victory is often attributed to the cynicism of politicians, but a good deal of it is built into the structure of the appeal. Vagueness borrows support from the future, and the future presents the bill. Nor is the critics' remedy as clean as it looks. A detailed platform has its own dishonesty, of a quieter kind. It implies a control over events that no government possesses, and its specific commitments are routinely overtaken by a recession, a war or some crisis that no one foresaw. A voter who holds a government to the letter of such a platform may end up rewarding rigidity over judgement. Specificity, in other words, can be as much a performance as vagueness is, a display of seriousness staged for an audience that has learned to distrust slogans. What, then, should a careful listener ask of political language? Not that it abandon general phrases, which coalitions cannot do without, nor that it supply a detailed plan for every contingency. A more useful question is whether the speaker, pressed on how the slogan would decide a real conflict between its own supporters, can name the principle that would settle it. A slogan backed by such a principle is simply a commitment stated at a high level of generality, and it can be held to account at that level. One that dissolves into a different answer for each audience that asks is merely a mirror, and it is the mirror, not the generality, that deserves the critics' contempt.
R08-D-08: Two stories are told about the anger that seems to pervade online discussion, and each is convenient for someone. In the first, the ranking systems that decide what appears in a feed have manufactured outrage, turning otherwise reasonable people into combatants. In the second, told chiefly by those who build such systems, a feed merely reflects its users: it shows people what they engage with, and if what they engage with is furious, the fault lies in human nature, not in the code. The first story flatters users, who become the victims of a machine; the second flatters engineers, who become the neutral servants of a public. Neither is quite right. Against the first story, it must be granted that outrage is old. Pamphleteers, broadsheets and street-corner orators discovered long before any computer that indignation sells, and audiences have always lingered over a scandal longer than over the correction that followed it. A ranking system that favours whatever holds attention did not invent this appetite. It found the appetite already there, and it could hardly have succeeded so quickly if it had not. Any account that treats the present climate as wholly unprecedented must therefore explain why the appetite it deplores appears so reliably in the commercial history of every earlier medium of mass communication. But the second story trades on an ambiguity in the word 'want'. A feed ranked by engagement learns what people react to: what they click, what they pause over, what they reply to in anger. Reaction is not the same as endorsement. A person may linger over a provocative post in the way a driver slows to look at an accident, and may say, if asked afterwards, that she wishes she had seen less of such material. A system that learns only from the lingering will give her more of it, and will describe the result as giving her what she wants. It is giving her what she wanted in the moment of reaction, which may be the opposite of what she wants on reflection. The older media of indignation differed in a further way that the mirror story overlooks. A newspaper editor chose what to print, but the feedback that reached him was slow and coarse, a matter of sales figures and letters to the editor. A feed reports, to every person who publishes in it, exactly how each post performed, often within minutes. Those who write for such an audience learn quickly which tone is rewarded, and many adjust accordingly, not because they are cynical but because they would like to be read. The ranking system therefore does not merely distribute a fixed supply of anger; it shapes the supply, by teaching producers what pays. A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror. It does not follow that the remedy is simply to rank posts by what people say, on reflection, that they value. Reflective preferences are harder to measure, easier to misreport and, when a platform infers them, open to the charge that the platform has substituted its own judgement for the user's. These are real objections, and they counsel modesty about any redesign. But they cut both ways. A system that optimises for momentary reaction has also made a judgement about what its users really want; it has simply made that judgement silently, and in favour of the version of the user that is easiest to count. Neutrality, in this domain, is not an available option; the only choice is between an explicit conception of the user's interests and an implicit one.
